title: TA8-17050
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: Sir, I am going to give you my decision and reasons at this time and these are the reasons that I am going to reject your claim.

The claimant is a 41-year-old male, habitually residing in Palestine and with a Jordanian travel document, which the claimant has testified does not give him the rights to reside in Jordan. He left Palestine most recently on two separate occasions and on both occasions, he went to the United States and on the second occasion, he left the United States and came to Canada where he made a refugee claim.

The basis of his refugee claim in Canada is that he fears persecution by the Israeli army if he was to return to Palestine and he has testified that he believes that he will be subject to more persecution than other Palestinian males because of some of the unique factors that he has experienced in the past. His oral evidence is that when his identity is checked and it is discovered that he is on a do not depart order and because of that status he has been forced to humiliate himself by barking like a dog and that he has been arrested. He believes that his home has been targeted because of his proximity to the gates of the refugee camp and as he outlines both in a personal information form filed with the board in October 2008, identified as C-1, and a second personal information form filed with the board in December 2008 that if he was to return the treatment that he has received in the past would continue and that this treatment would qualify him for the protection of Canada.

I will just note for the record that the October 2008 personal information form was signed on October 4 and the claimant indicated that it was complete, true and correct. The December 2008 personal information form was also signed indicating that it was complete, true and correct. There is a difference in the signatures; the December form is signed indicating that the claimant understands English and that he fully understands the contents of the form and it has the same force and effect as if made under oath. The earlier declaration indicates that the document had been interpreted to him but there is no interpreter's signature on that earlier document, but I am also satisfied that it would not be possible for the claimant to learn English and fully understand English in that month between October and December of 2008. Since he has signed that he does understand English in December I am satisfied on a balance of probability he also understood English in October.

So I am satisfied that the claimant has experienced discrimination as opposed to persecution in the past and that the claimant has not established that there is a serious possibility he will be persecuted should he return to Palestine today, for the following analysis:

In the claimant's oral evidence, he testified about his XXXX 2006 incident; the only recounted incident that occurred after his return to Palestine from the United States. He testified that some people are subjected to such treatment by the Israeli army more than others. He testified he believed that he was a person of that group. When asked why he thought that these kinds of treatments happened to him more often than to others he testified that he believed his name was on a no depart decree and then when Israeli officials checked his I.D. they would find his name on this no depart order. He believed his name was placed on this order sometime in 1991 when he was accused of being a member of the political liberation movement of Palestine. He went on to testify that he knew his name was on this order because he had gone to a military judge and that the intelligence services had placed his name on the list.

Initially he was asked why in the October personal information form there was no mention of his name being on that list and his testimony at that time was that his lawyer had already added this information. When it became known that a December amendment to the personal information form had been received by the board that document was checked and it also makes no mention of the claimant's name being on a do not depart list. The claimant explained that he knew his name was on that list because he had been recruited by the intelligence services of the Israeli army to operate as an agent for them and that information was not in the October version of his narrative. He explained it had been omitted because he had received advice to do the personal information form quickly and get it in within the 28 days, but I do not accept that getting it in quickly would negate the obligation to be complete, true and correct, an obligation that the claimant indicated on two separate occasions that he had fulfilled.

Further, the claimant did leave Palestine on a number of occasions and if we look at question 12 of the revised personal information form, C-1(a), we see that in 2004 he travelled to Egypt, in 2005 he travelled to Chicago in the United States and when I review all of the evidence I am satisfied that in fact on a balance of probability the claimant was due to the omission from both versions of his narrative, the evidence of him being able to travel on numerous occasions outside Palestine that on a balance of probability his name was not on a do not depart order.

In fact the claimant is, as he describes himself in paragraph 52 of C-1(a), where he talks about the reasons why he was jailed by the Israelis, he does not say that he was on a do not depart list, he says for no other reason than for being a male Palestinian, and I am satisfied that the claimant created the account of being on this special list in order to advance his refugee claim. I make a negative credibility inference as a result.

The claimant was safely in the United States XXXX, 2006 until XXXXXX, 2008 and returned to Palestine by way of Jordan. He testified that this re-availment was required in order to get visas for his children and that by returning he would show good faith to the U.S. authorities and this would assist in the obtainment of visas for the children. Now I find this re-availment inconsistent with his evidence that he believes he will be seriously harmed in Palestine. According to his narrative by the time he was in the United States he had experienced numerous actions of discrimination and feared for further such actions and in fact if we look at his revised personal information form in C-1(a), question 12, we see that from XXX of 2005 until XXXXXX 2005 he had gone to Chicago to escape from danger in Palestine and to be fair he does include that he had gone also for business considerations.

He had an opportunity to make a refugee claim when he was in the United States in 2005; he did not make such a claim. While I accept that, the United States might consider his return favourably in order to get visas for his children I do not accept that an individual who truly feared serious harm and persecution would put himself at the risk of such harm after being safely in the United States. I further note that a successful claim for asylum in the United States as it does in Canada would allow him to bring his children to the United States.

I further note that in the original version of the personal information form, C-1, when describing the purpose for his trip to the United States in 2005 he indicates that, in question 12, at line 12(h) that the purpose of that trip was for business and XXXXX. I am satisfied on a balance of probability that his answer in 12(h) of C-1 more probably indicates the true reason for his trip to the United States in 2005. As a result of the re-availment and the inconsistencies between that re-availment and his expressed fear of remaining in Palestine, I again make another negative credibility inference. I am satisfied that he created the answer in his amended personal information form in order to advance his refugee claim.

Counsel in his submissions indicated that I asked a question about a humiliating experience, the most humiliating experience that the claimant experienced prior to leaving Palestine. In fact, my notes show that the actual question was for the worst things that happened when you lived in Palestine, I did not use the word humiliation. However, I agree with counsel that he did describe an incident that would be of a humiliating nature, but humiliation is not normally on itself sufficient to establish persecution.

The evidence before me satisfies me that the claimant received an education when he lived in Palestine. According to his own evidence was employed throughout the period of time that he lived in Palestine. He had a residence, I agree it was at a refugee camp but he had a residence that he and his family and I guess his parents before him lived in. I am satisfied that his core human rights were not compromised when he lived in Palestine. He did testify that he experienced a rather horrific incident where his passenger in his truck was shot and killed, but according to his own evidence, he believed this was a random act and was not targeted at them particularly, but that in fact they were simply in the wrong place at the wrong time.

I considered whether his experiences cumulatively would amount to persecution. His own act of returning to Palestine in 2005 would support that he did not believe that he had been subjected to persecution prior to that. When I go through the long list of problems, perhaps the most serious might be the refusal to allow him to return to India to complete his schooling in 1991. However, he certainly was not deprived of schooling. In addition, since I have already found that he was not on a do not leave list I do not accept, the claimant has established the reason why he was not allowed to return to India. The claimant described the worst incident, the incident that occurred after he returned to Palestine when he was forced to stand and bark like a dog, but again I do not find that a single incident such as that would equate to a serious infringement of human rights as required to meet the level of persecution, on the balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the claimant has experienced discrimination because of his status as a Palestinian, but this discrimination does not reach the level of persecution. I have insufficient evidence before me to support that in the future there is a serious possibility the claimant will be persecuted if he was to return to Palestine. As a result, the claim fails pursuant to Section 96 of the Act.

The test for Section 97 is a higher test and the harm feared is more serious than that of persecution and so since I have found that the claimant has not established on the lower burden a risk of the less serious harm, I am satisfied the claimant has not established that it is more probable than not that he will experience the serious harm as envisioned by Section 97 of the Act, and hence the claim fails pursuant to Section 97 of the Act. As a result, the Refugee Protection Division rejects the claim.

That concludes the hearing. Thank you Mr. Interpreter as always, thank you counsel.
